lesson.title: Place by Place: Dividing 3-Digit Numbers

steps.say: You already know how to share a number into equal groups by chopping off friendly chunks. Today I will show you a tidy way to do it: divide one place at a time, starting from the left. Here is our problem: three classes share 936 dollars for a field trip, fairly. How much does each class get?

Watch how neat this is. Share the hundreds first: 9 hundreds shared by 3 is 3 hundreds. Then the tens: 3 tens shared by 3 is 1 ten. Then the ones: 6 ones shared by 3 is 2 ones. Put those pieces together and each class gets 312 dollars.

visual.caption: Split 936 by place, then divide each part by 3

steps.say: Let us check it, because checking is what good mathematicians do. Three groups of 312 dollars is 936 dollars, and that is exactly what we started with. Perfect.

visual.caption: Three equal shares of 312 dollars make 936 dollars

steps.say: Now a sneaky one. A berry farm packs 624 blueberries into 6 boxes, the same number in each box. Start with the hundreds: 6 hundreds shared by 6 is 1 hundred. Next the tens: we have only 2 tens, and 2 tens cannot be shared into 6 whole tens, so the tens answer is zero. Write that zero down and slide the 2 tens over to the ones, making 24 ones. Then 24 shared by 6 is 4. Each box gets 104 blueberries.

visual.caption: 600 divided by 6 is 100, and 24 divided by 6 is 4

steps.say: Here is the mistake almost everybody makes once. Some kids skip that empty tens spot and write 14 instead of 104. But look what happens: 6 boxes with 14 blueberries each is only 84 blueberries, nowhere near 624. That little zero is not nothing, it is a placeholder holding the tens spot open so the 1 stays in the hundreds. Never skip it.

visual.caption: Dropping the zero makes the answer far too small

steps.say: So remember: divide hundreds, then tens, then ones, and if a place gives you nothing, write a zero right there and keep going.

visual.caption: 1 hundred, 0 tens, 4 ones — the zero holds the tens place

lesson.answer: Divide place by place, left to right — and when a place gives nothing, write a zero there and keep going.

practice.question: An apple stand in Kelowna has 728 apples and packs them into 7 crates, with the same number of apples in every crate. Draw 7 equal groups if it helps you picture it. How many apples go in each crate? Try dividing the hundreds first, then the tens, then the ones — and watch out for a place that gives nothing!
practice.answer: 104 apples in each crate. Here is why: 7 hundreds shared by 7 is 1 hundred; only 2 tens are left, which cannot make whole tens for 7 groups, so the tens digit is 0; then those 2 tens plus the 8 ones make 28 ones, and 28 divided by 7 is 4. Check it: 7 times 104 is 728.
